opus-5.5.text:
I think the common thread is actually quite simple: we want to get more intelligence per unit of compute, and per unit of memory bandwidth. Architecture research, at least the kind I care about, is really about efficiency. It's not about inventing some magical new inductive bias that suddenly makes the model smarter. It's about making the model cheaper to train and cheaper to serve, so that for the same budget you can scale further.

If you look at fine-grained MoE, the idea is that you decouple the number of parameters from the amount of compute per token. A dense model has to touch every parameter for every token, which is very wasteful. With MoE, and especially fine-grained MoE where you have many small experts and activate a handful of them, you can have a huge parameter count, so a lot of knowledge capacity, while each token only pays for a small slice. DeepSeek showed quite convincingly that making the experts smaller and more numerous gives you better combinatorial flexibility and better specialization. So MoE is mainly attacking the FLOPs side of the problem, the MLP side.

Efficient attention attacks a different bottleneck, which is the sequence dimension. Standard softmax attention costs quadratic compute in training, and at inference the KV cache grows linearly with context length. Decoding becomes memory-bound: you're constantly loading this huge KV cache from HBM just to produce one token. Now that we care about long-context reasoning, agents running long trajectories, and RL with very long rollouts, that cost really dominates. So things like linear attention, state space models, DeltaNet-style models, sparse attention, and hybrids that mix a few global attention layers with many linear layers are all trying to make long sequences affordable: constant memory per layer for the recurrent part, much better throughput at long context.

So I'd say MoE makes the model "wider" cheaply, and efficient attention makes it "longer" cheaply. Together they define the efficiency frontier.

One thing I always emphasize is that efficiency has to be real on hardware. A lot of earlier work on efficient attention had good theoretical complexity but ran slower than FlashAttention in practice, because it didn't use tensor cores well or wasn't parallelizable in training. That's why much of my own work has been about hardware-efficient algorithms, like chunkwise parallel forms for linear attention and DeltaNet, so you can train these models at the same speed as transformers. If the kernel isn't fast, nobody will adopt the architecture, however elegant the math.

The other side is that you can't just trade away quality. Pure linear attention historically struggled with recall and in-context retrieval, because you're compressing everything into a fixed-size state. So the goal is to find the best trade-off: better state update rules, like the delta rule and gating, so the fixed-size memory is used more intelligently, and then hybrid designs where a small amount of full attention covers the precise retrieval. I think that's where the field is converging. It isn't "attention is dead," it's using expensive global attention only where you really need it.

So, in one sentence: the goal is to push the Pareto frontier of capability versus cost, in training and especially in inference, because in the era of test-time scaling, inference efficiency is becoming the thing that determines how far you can go.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the goal is really simple at the core: we want to get more intelligence per unit of compute, and per unit of memory. Scaling laws tell us that if you throw more FLOPs and more data at a transformer, it gets better, but the actual constraint we face is that compute and memory bandwidth are finite and expensive. So architecture research is about changing the shape of the model so that each FLOP, and especially each byte you move through the GPU, buys you more capability.

Fine-grained MoE and efficient attention attack two different bottlenecks. MoE is mostly about the FFN side. In a dense model, every token activates every parameter, which is wasteful, because a given token probably only needs a small slice of the knowledge stored in the weights. Mixture of experts decouples the total parameter count from the active compute per token. The "fine-grained" part, like what DeepSeek did with many small experts and shared experts, is about making the routing more flexible, so you get better specialization and combinatorial coverage without increasing the active FLOPs. You can store a lot of knowledge in the model while keeping inference cheap.

Attention is a different story. The problem with softmax attention is not really training compute, it's the KV cache at inference. The cost grows linearly with sequence length for every decoded token, and that becomes a memory-bandwidth problem, not a FLOPs problem. So the work on linear attention, state-space models, gated variants, DeltaNet-style updates, and also things like MLA or sparse attention, are all trying to compress that state. You want a fixed-size or much smaller memory that still retains the information that matters. The interesting research question there is how to make the recurrent state expressive enough, with good update and forgetting rules, so you don't lose the in-context retrieval ability that full attention gives you for free.

And then, honestly, the hidden half of this work is hardware-awareness. An architecture only counts as efficient if it maps well onto GPUs: you need to be able to chunk the computation into matmuls, keep things in SRAM, and write a kernel that actually runs fast. A lot of ideas look elegant on paper but die because they can't be parallelized across the sequence. So I see architecture design as co-design: the algorithm, the hardware, and the kernel have to be thought about together.

The longer-term goal, to me, is that these things compose. A hybrid model with fine-grained MoE for capacity, a mostly-linear attention backbone for cheap long context, and a few full attention layers for precise retrieval, could give you something that scales much better on both axes. We're not at the end of that, but I think that's the direction.

astra-6.text:
I think the goal is to use a limited compute budget more effectively. There are two complementary directions: make the model more capable for the same cost, or preserve its capability while reducing the cost of training and inference.

Fine-grained MoE tries to achieve this through conditional computation. You can give the model a large pool of parameters, but activate only a small subset for each token. The important question is whether that flexibility translates into better performance after accounting for routing, communication, and hardware utilization.

More efficient attention addresses how the model accesses information across tokens. If we can reduce the computation or memory needed for that interaction while preserving the information the task requires, we can support longer contexts or make inference cheaper.

So I would judge these innovations by the capability they deliver under real resource constraints. A better theoretical complexity is useful, but ultimately it needs to translate into a better system.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the goal is to get more intelligence out of a given compute budget. Fine-grained MoE and more efficient attention approach that from different directions.

With MoE, you can increase the model’s total capacity without activating every parameter for every token. Making the experts more fine-grained gives you more flexibility in how you allocate that computation. But you also have to account for routing, communication, and whether the hardware can execute it efficiently.

For attention, the question is how to use context effectively without letting the cost of reading and storing that context become overwhelming. Ideally, you reduce that cost while preserving the information the model needs.

So I would judge these innovations by the capability they deliver at a real training or inference budget. A lower theoretical operation count is useful, but ultimately it has to translate into a better model or a cheaper system in practice.
